intro: For more than two thousand years, students across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam learned from the same small library. It held the Five Classics and, later, the Four Books. Officials had to know them. Poets quoted them. Families argued over them at dinner.

In this unit you will open that library. You will learn what each of the Five Classics is and how Zhu Xi built the Four Books. You will look inside the Analects to see how it was put together. Then you will follow a great debate inside the Confucian tradition: Mencius and Xunzi on whether human nature is good.

By the end, you will be able to name the classics and their genres, read a citation like Mencius 2A.6, and explain both sides of the human nature debate. You will use the words of the texts themselves as your evidence.
bigQuestion: What did the Confucian classics teach, and why did their readers argue about them?

write.prompt: Is human nature good? Explain how Mencius and Xunzi answer. Cite Mencius 2A.6 and 6A.2 (Legge, 1895) and Xunzi ch. 23 (paraphrased), and describe how Zhu Xi and later readers took sides or kept both.
tips: Cite each passage with its book and number, like Mencius 2A.6.
Attribute every view: "Mencius argued..." or "Xunzi claimed..."
Explain each image, such as the sprout or the warped board.
Compare the two thinkers rather than naming a winner.
Use unit words like human nature, four sprouts and conscious effort.

title: The Confucian Classics

chapters.title: Four Books and Five Classics
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a set of old books become the shared education of East Asia for centuries?

story.title: Four Hundred Thousand Characters
story.kicker: A boy in the year 1500 begins the long climb toward the imperial exam.
paragraphs: It is the year 1500, in a town south of the Yangzi River. Eight-year-old Wenming sits at a low desk before dawn. His teacher reads a line from the Analects aloud. Wenming repeats it, again and again, rocking gently to the rhythm, until he can say it without looking.

His family has saved for years to pay this teacher. If Wenming passes the imperial exams, he may become an official. That would bring honor and security to his parents, his grandparents' memory and his whole clan. If he fails, the savings may be gone.

The task is huge. Over the coming years he must memorize the Four Books and the Five Classics. Together they hold more than 400,000 characters. He must also learn the commentary of the scholar Zhu Xi, because the exam expects answers in Zhu Xi's reading.

Not everyone thinks this is the point of learning. Wenming's teacher tells him that Confucius studied to improve himself, not to impress others. Wenming nods, then goes back to his recitation. Outside, the rooster crows. He has only begun.
story.think: What might Wenming gain from memorizing the classics? What might he miss?

lessons.title: A Library of Five
lessons.mainIdea: The Five Classics are five ancient books of poetry, history, divination, ritual and chronicle that Han scholars made the core of learning.
reading: A *canon* is a set of books that a community treats as its most important texts. In Han China, the canon was the *Five Classics*. They were the Book of Songs, the Book of Documents, the Book of Changes, the Book of Rites and the Spring and Autumn Annals.

Each is a different *genre*, or kind of writing. The Songs is poetry. The Documents is speeches and records from early kings. The Changes is a divination book. The Rites describes ceremonies and conduct. The Spring and Autumn is a short year-by-year chronicle of the state of Lu.

Tradition held that Confucius edited or wrote some of these books. Modern scholars think most are older or later than Confucius, and grew over time. What is clear is that from the Han on, officials were expected to know them well.

words.d: the set of books a community treats as its most important texts
the Songs, Documents, Changes, Rites and Spring and Autumn Annals
a kind of writing, such as poetry, history or dialogue

look.title: Sizes of the Five Classics
look.cite: Standard received texts; Spring and Autumn covers 722–481 BCE
look.prompt: What does each number count? Why can't you compare these three numbers directly?

check.q: Which of the Five Classics is poetry?
check.why: The Book of Songs (Shijing) is a collection of 305 poems.

check.q: What is a canon?
choices: A community's set of most important texts
check.why: A canon is the set of books a community treats as central.

check.q: What do modern scholars think about Confucius and the Five Classics?
choices: He wrote all of them himself
Most grew over time, before and after him
check.why: Scholars see the Five Classics as layered texts older and later than Confucius.

lessons.title: The Book of Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Songs gathers 305 early poems, and Confucian readers used them to teach feeling, speech and virtue.
reading: The *Book of Songs* (*Shijing*) holds 305 poems, most from about 1000 to 600 BCE. Some are folk songs about love, farming and soldiers far from home. Others are hymns sung at court and at ancestral temples.

The first poem, "Guan ju," pictures ospreys calling on a river island and a young man longing for a gentle lady. Han commentators read it as praise of a queen's virtue. Many modern readers read it as a love song. The same poem, two readings.

Confucius valued the Songs highly. In Analects 17.9, he tells students the Songs can stir the mind, help them observe, help them get along with others, and teach them duties to father and ruler. In Analects 2.2, he sums up all 300 poems in one phrase: no twisted thoughts.

words.d: the Shijing, a collection of 305 early Chinese poems; one of the Five Classics
notes that explain a text, often written by later scholars
a song of praise used in worship or ceremony

look.title: The Songs in One Phrase
look.text: In the Book of Poetry are three hundred pieces, but the design of them all may be embraced in one sentence — 'Having no depraved thoughts.'
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 2.2, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: Confucius says 'three hundred' though there are 305. What does that tell you about how he is speaking?

check.q: How many poems are in the Book of Songs?
check.why: The Shijing holds 305 poems; Confucius rounds to 300 in Analects 2.2.

check.q: How did Han commentators read the poem 'Guan ju'?
choices: As praise of a queen's virtue
check.why: Han commentators read 'Guan ju' morally, as praise of a queen; many modern readers see a love song.

check.q: In Analects 2.2, how does Confucius sum up the Songs?
check.why: Legge's 2.2 has Confucius sum up the Songs as 'Having no depraved thoughts.'

lessons.title: Documents, Changes and Rites
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Documents records early rulers, the Book of Changes is a divination text with commentaries, and the Book of Rites sets out ritual and its meaning.
reading: The *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*) gathers speeches and announcements credited to early kings and ministers, including the Zhou speeches on the Mandate of Heaven. As you learned, some chapters were later forgeries, which scholars sorted out over centuries.

The *Book of Changes* (*Yijing*, or I Ching) began as a divination manual. It uses 64 *hexagrams*, figures of six broken or solid lines. People cast yarrow stalks or coins to choose one, then read its text. Later commentaries, the "Ten Wings," turned it into a book of philosophy about change, yin and yang.

The *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) explains ceremonies from mourning to archery, and why they matter. Two of its chapters, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, would later become two of the Four Books.

words.d: the Yijing or I Ching, a divination book of 64 hexagrams with philosophical commentaries
a figure of six stacked lines, broken or solid, used in the Book of Changes
a practice of seeking guidance or knowledge of what is hidden, such as by casting lots
the Liji, a classic on ceremonies and their meaning

look.title: Six Lines
look.text: Picture a hexagram: six horizontal lines stacked on top of one another. Some are solid. Some are broken in the middle. Two possibilities for each of six lines make 64 different figures. Each figure has a name, a short text and notes on each line.
look.prompt: Why do 2 choices for each of 6 lines make 64 figures? How might a divination book become a book of philosophy?

check.q: How many hexagrams are in the Book of Changes?
check.why: The Yijing has 64 hexagrams, the possible figures of six lines.

check.q: Which of the Four Books came from chapters of the Book of Rites?
choices: The Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean
check.why: Both were chapters of the Liji before Zhu Xi grouped them into the Four Books.

check.q: What were the 'Ten Wings'?
choices: Commentaries that turned the Changes into philosophy
check.why: The Ten Wings are commentaries on the Yijing that read it as a philosophy of change.

lessons.title: Zhu Xi's Four Books
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1100s, Zhu Xi grouped the Analects, Mencius, Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean as the Four Books and wrote commentaries on them.
reading: *Zhu Xi* (1130–1200) was a scholar of the Song dynasty. He wanted a clear path into Confucian learning. So he grouped four texts as the *Four Books*: the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean.

Zhu Xi advised students to read them in a set order: first the Great Learning for the outline, then the Analects for the foundation, then the Mencius, and last the Doctrine of the Mean for its depth. He wrote detailed notes on all four and published them together in 1190.

His reading shaped centuries of study. In 1313, the Yuan government made his commentary the standard for the civil-service exams. It stayed the standard until the exams ended in 1905. Later thinkers, like Wang Yangming, challenged parts of his reading.

words.d: Song dynasty scholar (1130–1200) who grouped and annotated the Four Books
the Analects, Mencius, Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean, grouped by Zhu Xi

look.title: About How Long Are the Four Books?
look.cite: Rounded from counts given in Ichisada Miyazaki, China's Examination Hell (Eng. trans. 1976)
look.prompt: Which book is longest? Why might Zhu Xi start students with the shortest?

check.q: Who grouped the Four Books?
check.why: Zhu Xi (1130–1200) grouped and annotated the Four Books.

check.q: In what year did Zhu Xi's commentary become the exam standard?
check.why: The Yuan government made his commentary the exam standard in 1313.

check.q: Which book did Zhu Xi tell students to read first?
check.why: Zhu Xi advised starting with the Great Learning as an outline.

lessons.title: The Great Learning and the Mean
lessons.mainIdea: The Great Learning links personal growth to good government, and the Doctrine of the Mean describes balance and sincerity.
reading: The *Great Learning* is short. Its most famous passage traces a chain: to bring peace to the world, first govern the state well; to do that, first order the family; to do that, first cultivate yourself; and to do that, first set your heart right and make your thoughts sincere.

The *Doctrine of the Mean* (*Zhongyong*) is about balance, or *zhong*. It describes a state in which feelings are not yet stirred and then, when they arise, hit the right measure. It also stresses *cheng*, sincerity or being true, which it links to the Way of Heaven.

Both texts are paraphrased here, since the public-domain translations named for this course do not include them. Tradition credits the Mean to Confucius's grandson Zisi. Many modern scholars date both texts to the late Warring States or early Han.

words.d: a short text linking self-cultivation to family order and good government
the Zhongyong, a text on balance and sincerity
working over time to improve one's own character

look.title: The Chain of the Great Learning
look.text: Those who wished to bring order to the world first ordered their states. Wishing to order their states, they first set their families in order. Wishing to set their families in order, they first cultivated themselves. Wishing to cultivate themselves, they first made their hearts right.
look.cite: Great Learning, opening section, paraphrased; see Wing-tsit Chan, A Source Book in Chinese Philosophy (1963)
look.prompt: Where does the chain begin and where does it end? What does it suggest about leaders?

check.q: In the Great Learning, what comes before ordering the family?
check.why: The Great Learning puts self-cultivation before ordering the family.

check.q: What is a key idea of the Doctrine of the Mean?
check.why: The Zhongyong centers on zhong (balance) and cheng (sincerity).

check.q: To whom does tradition credit the Doctrine of the Mean?
check.why: Tradition credits it to Zisi; many modern scholars date it later.

lessons.title: The Mencius as a Book
lessons.mainIdea: The Mencius is a book of conversations between Mencius and rulers, students and rivals, arranged in seven books.
reading: The *Mencius* is named for the thinker Mengzi, or Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE). It is much longer than the Analects. Many passages are full conversations, where Mencius argues with kings, students and rival thinkers.

The book has seven books, each divided into two parts. Scholars cite them as 1A, 1B, 2A and so on. So Mencius 2A.6 means book 2, part A, passage 6. Legge's translation labels the parts "Part I" and "Part II" and uses titles from the book's rulers and students.

The Mencius was not always in the canon. For centuries it was read as one philosopher among many. It rose in status during the Song dynasty, and Zhu Xi's Four Books made it central. The next chapter looks closely at its ideas.

words.d: Mengzi (c. 372–289 BCE), a Confucian thinker; also the book of his conversations
a written conversation between two or more speakers

look.title: Reading a Citation
look.text: A textbook cites 'Mencius 6A.2.' Another cites 'Mencius, Book VI, Part I, chapter 2 (Legge).' A third cites 'Mengzi 6A2.'
look.prompt: Are these the same passage? Explain how to read each form.

check.q: What does 'Mencius 2A.6' mean?
check.why: Mencius is cited by book, part (A or B) and passage number.

check.q: How does the Mencius differ from the Analects in form?
check.why: The Mencius has extended dialogues, while the Analects has many short sayings.

check.q: When did the Mencius rise to canonical status?
check.why: The Mencius rose in status during the Song, and Zhu Xi made it one of the Four Books.

lessons.title: How the Analects Is Built
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects is a collection of short sayings and scenes in 20 books, gathered by students over time rather than written by Confucius.
reading: Open the Analects anywhere and you find short entries. Many begin, "The Master said." Others show a student asking a question, or describe how Confucius dressed and ate. The book has 20 books and roughly 500 passages. Editions number some passages differently.

Confucius did not write it. The Chinese title, *Lunyu*, means something like "selected sayings." His students, and their students, gathered the material. Most scholars agree it reached roughly its present form by the early Han.

Scholars debate its *layers*. Some argue that books 3 to 9 hold older material and that the last books were added later. Others think the evidence is too thin to be sure. Readers can still notice that some books feel different from others.

words.d: the Chinese title of the Analects, meaning roughly selected sayings
parts of a text added at different times
to gather material from different sources into one book

look.title: The Opening Lines
look.text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 1.1, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: Why might the compilers have chosen these lines to open the whole book?

check.q: Who wrote down the Analects?
check.why: The Analects was compiled by Confucius's students and later followers.

check.q: What does 'Lunyu' roughly mean?
check.why: Lunyu, the Chinese title, means roughly selected or ordered sayings.

check.q: What do scholars debate about the Analects?
choices: Whether it has layers from different times
check.why: Scholars debate which books are older and which were added later.

lessons.title: Sayings, Dialogues and Scenes
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects mixes short sayings, question-and-answer dialogues and scenes, and each genre asks readers to read differently.
reading: Some Analects passages are *sayings*: one sentence to think about. "The Master said" introduces a thought, with no setting. Readers must imagine when, why and to whom it was said. That open space is one reason commentaries grew so long.

Other passages are dialogues. In Analects 12.1, the student Yan Hui asks about ren, humaneness. Confucius answers that it means mastering oneself and returning to ritual. Different students ask the same question and get different answers. Many readers think he fitted each answer to the student.

Book 10 is mostly *scenes*. It describes how Confucius behaved at court, at home and at meals. He would not sit on a mat that was not straight. These details show ritual as part of daily life, not only temple ceremony.

words.d: a short statement of an idea, often without a setting
a description of a person's actions in a setting

look.title: Same Question, Different Answers
look.text: In Analects 12.1, Yan Hui asks about ren; Confucius tells him to master himself and return to ritual. In 12.2, Zhonggong asks; Confucius tells him not to do to others what he would not want done to himself. In 12.22, Fan Chi asks; Confucius says: love others.
look.prompt: Why might a teacher give three students three answers to one question? What does this suggest about ren?

check.q: What does Analects book 10 mostly contain?
check.why: Book 10 describes how Confucius acted at court, at home and at meals.

check.q: In Analects 12.22, how does Confucius describe ren to Fan Chi?
check.why: Confucius tells Fan Chi that ren means to love others.

check.q: Why might Confucius give students different answers about ren?
choices: He fitted each answer to the student
check.why: Many readers think Confucius tailored answers to each student's needs.

lessons.title: Canons Beyond China
lessons.mainIdea: Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese scholars also studied the Four Books and Five Classics, writing their own commentaries.
reading: The classics did not stay inside China. In Korea, Silla and later Goryeo and Joseon rulers set up schools and exams on the classics. The Joseon dynasty (1392–1910) made Zhu Xi's learning its official philosophy.

In Japan, scholars studied the classics for centuries. In the Tokugawa period (1603–1868), schools of Confucian thought flourished, and some scholars, such as Ito Jinsai, argued with Zhu Xi's reading. Vietnam held exams on the classics from 1075 until 1919.

Because the classics were written in classical Chinese, educated people across East Asia could read the same *texts* even when they spoke different languages. Each country also built its own *interpretation*.

words.d: an explanation of what a text means
a Korean dynasty (1392–1910) that made Zhu Xi's Confucian learning official
the written language of the classics, read across East Asia

look.title: Exams on the Classics Ended
look.cite: Standard dates in East Asian histories
look.prompt: Which country ended the exams last? What changes around 1900 might explain these dates?

check.q: Which Korean dynasty made Zhu Xi's learning official?
check.why: Joseon Korea (1392–1910) adopted Zhu Xi's Confucianism as its official learning.

check.q: Why could scholars across East Asia read the same classics?
check.why: Classical Chinese served as a shared written language across East Asia.

check.q: When did Vietnam end its exams on the classics?
check.why: Vietnam's classical exams ran until 1919.

review.q: Which is NOT one of the Five Classics?
review.why: The Analects is one of the Four Books, not the Five Classics.

review.q: Which classic is a year-by-year chronicle of Lu?
review.why: The Spring and Autumn Annals records events in Lu, 722–481 BCE.

review.q: Who grouped the Four Books in the 1100s?
review.why: Zhu Xi grouped the Four Books and published his commentary in 1190.

review.q: Which pair of Four Books came from the Book of Rites?
choices: Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean
review.why: The Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean were chapters of the Liji.

review.q: What genre is the Book of Changes?
review.why: The Yijing is a divination text later read as philosophy through the Ten Wings.

review.q: What does the Great Learning put first in its chain?
choices: Setting the heart right and cultivating oneself
review.why: The Great Learning traces order back to self-cultivation and a right heart.

choices: Written by Confucius in one year
Compiled by his students over time
review.why: The Analects was gathered by students and later followers, probably in layers.

review.q: Why did the exam in 1500 require Zhu Xi's commentary?
choices: It had been the exam standard since 1313
It was the only book left
review.why: From 1313, Zhu Xi's commentary was the official standard for exam answers.

chapters.title: Mencius and Xunzi: Is Human Nature Good?
chapters.bigQuestion: Are people born with the seeds of goodness, or do they become good only through shaping?

story.title: Two Teachers, One Child
story.kicker: Two Confucian teachers watch the same crying child and draw opposite lessons.
paragraphs: Imagine a market square in the state of Qi, around 300 BCE. A small child has wandered from her mother and stands near an open well, crying. A stranger drops his basket, runs over and pulls her back from the edge. The crowd lets out its breath.

An older teacher watches. For him, the moment proves something. The stranger did not stop to think about reward or praise. He simply felt alarm and moved. "There," the teacher tells his students. "Every person has a heart that cannot bear to see others suffer. Goodness is already in us, like a sprout."

A younger scholar sees the same crowd differently. He notices two boys squabbling over the stranger's spilled fruit. "Look," he says. "Left alone, people grab. The stranger acted well because he was raised well. Goodness comes from teachers, rituals and practice, the way a craftsman straightens a warped board."

These two voices stand for real thinkers. The first sounds like Mencius. The second sounds like Xunzi. Both called themselves followers of Confucius. Yet they gave opposite answers to one of the oldest questions in philosophy.
story.think: Which part of the scene would you point to as evidence for each teacher's view?

lessons.title: The Child at the Well
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius argued that everyone has a heart that cannot bear others' suffering, shown by instant alarm at a child about to fall into a well.
reading: Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE) lived about a century after Confucius. Tradition says he studied with students of Confucius's grandson. Like Confucius, he traveled to advise rulers. The book named for him records his arguments.

His most famous argument is in Mencius 2A.6. Suppose someone suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well. They will feel alarm and *compassion*. Mencius says this is not to win the parents' friendship or neighbors' praise, or because they dislike the child's cry. The feeling comes on its own.

From this, Mencius concludes that the heart of compassion is part of being human. Someone without it, he says, is not fully human. This is a *thought experiment*, an imagined case used to test an idea. Readers still debate whether it proves what he claims.

words.d: feeling for others' suffering and wanting to help
an imagined case used to test an idea
what people are like at birth, before training; in Chinese, xing

look.title: A Mind That Cannot Bear Suffering
look.text: All men have a mind which cannot bear to see the sufferings of others.
look.cite: Mencius 2A.6, trans. James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: How does the child-at-the-well case try to support this claim? Is one case enough?

check.q: In Mencius 2A.6, what does the person who sees the child feel?
check.why: Mencius says anyone would feel alarm and distress on seeing the child near the well.

check.q: What reason for the feeling does Mencius rule out?
choices: Wanting praise or the parents' friendship
check.why: Mencius says the feeling is not for friendship, praise or dislike of the cry.

check.q: What is a thought experiment?
choices: An imagined case used to test an idea
check.why: The child at the well is an imagined case Mencius uses to test his claim.

lessons.title: Four Sprouts of Virtue
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius taught that four inborn feelings are the sprouts of four virtues, which grow when they are cared for.
reading: In the same passage, 2A.6, Mencius names four feelings. The feeling of compassion is the start of *ren*, humaneness. The feeling of shame is the start of *yi*, rightness. The feeling of modesty and yielding is the start of *li*, ritual propriety. The sense of right and wrong is the start of *zhi*, wisdom.

The Chinese word Mencius uses, duan, can mean a beginning, a tip or a *sprout*. Many translators choose "sprout" to show his picture. Virtue is not complete at birth. It is a small shoot that can grow into a tree, or be crushed.

Mencius says people have these four as they have four limbs. If they extend them, it is like a fire starting to burn or a spring starting to flow. If they neglect them, they cannot even serve their parents.

words.d: Mencius's four inborn feelings that begin the virtues of ren, yi, li and zhi
rightness; doing what is fitting and just
wisdom; knowing right from wrong
humaneness; caring for others

look.title: The Four Principles
look.text: The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence. The feeling of shame and dislike is the principle of righteousness. The feeling of modesty and complying is the principle of propriety. The feeling of approving and disapproving is the principle of knowledge.
look.cite: Mencius 2A.6, trans. James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: Legge translates duan as 'principle'; others use 'sprout' or 'beginning.' How does each word change the meaning?

check.q: According to Mencius, compassion is the sprout of which virtue?
check.why: Mencius says compassion is the beginning of ren, humaneness.

check.q: Why do many translators use the word 'sprout'?
choices: It shows virtue begins small and must grow
check.why: Sprout captures Mencius's picture of virtue as a beginning that needs care to grow.

check.q: What does Mencius say happens if people neglect the sprouts?
choices: They cannot even serve their parents
check.why: In 2A.6 Mencius says those who do not develop them cannot even serve their parents.

lessons.title: Ox Mountain and the Farmer of Song
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius used stories of a stripped mountain and an impatient farmer to explain why goodness can be lost and how it grows.
reading: If people are good by nature, why do so many act badly? Mencius answers with a picture in 6A.8. The trees on Ox Mountain were once lovely. But people cut them with axes, and cattle and sheep grazed the new shoots. Now the mountain is bare, and people think it never had trees.

Human beings are like this, Mencius says. The good heart is cut down day after day. But each night, and in the calm of early morning, a little goodness grows back. Bad conduct cuts it down again. Its *nature* was never bare.

In 2A.2, Mencius tells of a farmer of Song who worried his grain was growing slowly, so he pulled on every sprout. He came home tired and boasted he had helped them grow. His son ran to look; the plants had withered. Moral growth, Mencius suggests, cannot be forced, but it cannot be ignored either.

words.d: what something is like at its root; for Mencius, human nature tends toward good
to care for something so it grows, like a plant or a virtue

look.title: The Bare Mountain
look.text: Picture a hill outside a city. Its slopes are bare and brown. An old woman tells you: 'When I was a girl, oaks and pines covered it. Then came the axes and the goats. Look closely, though: after each rain, green shoots still push up between the rocks.'
look.prompt: How does Mencius use this kind of picture to answer the question: 'If people are good, why do so many do wrong?'

check.q: What happened to Ox Mountain in Mencius 6A.8?
check.why: Axes and grazing animals stripped the mountain, though it once had trees.

check.q: What mistake did the farmer of Song make?
choices: He pulled the sprouts to make them grow faster
check.why: In Mencius 2A.2, he pulled at his sprouts and they withered.

check.q: What lesson do many readers take from the farmer of Song?
check.why: Mencius uses the story to show that virtue must be nurtured, not forced.

lessons.title: The People Come First
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius taught that the people matter more than the ruler, and that a ruler who cares for them will win their hearts.
reading: Mencius spoke boldly to kings. In 7B.14 he ranks what matters in a state: the people first, the altars of the land and grain next, and the ruler last. Few thinkers of his time said such a thing to a ruler's face.

He urged *humane government*. A king should lower taxes, not waste the people's labor in farming seasons, and make sure the old do not go hungry. In 1A.7 he tells King Xuan of Qi that the king's own pity for an ox being led to sacrifice shows he has the heart to rule well.

Mencius believed that a ruler who shows care wins the people's hearts, and that such a ruler cannot be stopped. He connected this to the Mandate of Heaven: Heaven sees as the people see, a line he quotes from the Book of Documents.

words.d: rule that cares for the people's needs; Mencius's ideal
the idea that Heaven grants the right to rule and can withdraw it

look.title: The People and the Sovereign
look.text: The people are the most important element in a nation; the spirits of the land and grain are the next; the sovereign is the lightest.
look.cite: Mencius 7B.14, trans. James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: Why was this a bold thing to say in a kingdom? How might a king react?

check.q: In Mencius 7B.14, what matters most in a state?
check.why: Mencius ranks the people first and the sovereign last.

check.q: What did King Xuan's pity for an ox show, according to Mencius?
choices: He had the heart to rule humanely
check.why: In 1A.7, Mencius says the king's pity shows he has the heart for humane government.

check.q: What line does Mencius quote from the Book of Documents?
choices: Heaven sees as the people see
check.why: Mencius cites the Documents: Heaven sees and hears as the people do.

lessons.title: When a Ruler Loses the Mandate
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius argued that a cruel ruler loses the right to be called a ruler, a claim later readers used both to limit and to challenge power.
reading: In Mencius 1B.8, King Xuan asks whether it was right for the founders of Shang and Zhou to overthrow the kings before them. Was that not a subject killing his ruler? Mencius answers that one who destroys humaneness and rightness is a mere *tyrant*, a 'fellow.' He has heard of killing the fellow Zhou, the last Shang king, but not of killing a ruler.
The point is sharp. A ruler who is cruel to the people has already stopped being a true ruler. The Mandate of Heaven has passed from him. Some later readers called this a right of *rebellion*.

Rulers noticed. Tradition reports that the first Ming emperor, in the 1300s, was angered by such passages and had an edited Mencius prepared with some passages removed. Scholars also debate how far Mencius meant to go; he did not call on ordinary people to rise up.

words.d: a cruel ruler who uses power for himself and harms the people
rising up against a ruler or government

look.title: The Fellow Zhou
look.text: King Xuan asks if a minister may kill his ruler. Mencius replies that a man who injures humaneness and rightness is only a fellow. He has heard of the cutting off of the fellow Zhou, but not of the killing of a sovereign.
look.cite: Mencius 1B.8, paraphrased from James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: How does Mencius change the question by renaming the king? Why might later emperors dislike this passage?

check.q: In Mencius 1B.8, what does Mencius call a cruel king?
check.why: Mencius says one who destroys humaneness and rightness is only a 'fellow,' not a true ruler.

check.q: What did the first Ming emperor reportedly do?
choices: Had passages removed from an edition
check.why: Tradition reports he ordered an edited Mencius with passages he disliked cut out.

check.q: What do scholars debate about 1B.8?
choices: How far Mencius meant to go in allowing rebellion
Whether it was written by Xunzi
check.why: Scholars debate whether Mencius endorsed rebellion broadly or only in extreme cases.

lessons.title: Mencius Debates Gaozi
lessons.mainIdea: In Mencius 6A, Mencius argues with Gaozi, who said human nature is neither good nor bad, using images of willow wood and water.
reading: Book 6A opens with a debate. The thinker Gaozi says human nature is like willow wood, and rightness is like cups and bowls. Making people good is like carving the wood. Mencius replies: do you follow the willow's nature, or must you do violence to it? If violence, then you say goodness harms human nature.

Gaozi tries another image. Human nature is like water whirling in a pool. Open a channel east and it flows east; open one west and it flows west. So nature is neither good nor bad. Mencius answers in 6A.2 that water may not prefer east or west, but it always flows down.

Water can be splashed over your head or forced uphill, Mencius adds, but that is force, not its nature. So it is with people who do wrong. This *debate* shows how carefully early thinkers built arguments with *analogies*.

words.d: a thinker who debated Mencius, arguing that human nature is neither good nor bad
a comparison that explains one thing by pointing to another that is similar

look.title: Water Flows Down
look.text: The tendency of man's nature to good is like the tendency of water to flow downwards. There are none but have this tendency to good, just as all water flows downwards.
look.cite: Mencius 6A.2, trans. James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: How does Mencius turn Gaozi's water image against him? Is the analogy convincing? Why?

check.q: What did Gaozi say about human nature?
choices: It is neither good nor bad
check.why: Gaozi compared nature to whirling water that can flow either way.

check.q: How does Mencius answer the water image?
choices: Water always flows down, as nature tends to good
check.why: In 6A.2 Mencius says nature tends to good as water tends to flow down.

check.q: What is an analogy?
choices: A comparison that explains one thing through another
check.why: The willow and water images are analogies used to argue about human nature.

lessons.title: Human Nature Is Bad
lessons.mainIdea: Xunzi argued that human nature is bad, meaning inborn desires lead to conflict, and that goodness comes from deliberate effort.
reading: *Xunzi* (c. 310–235 BCE) was the leading Confucian of the late Warring States. He taught at the Jixia Academy in Qi, and later lived in the state of Chu. Tradition says Han Feizi and Li Si studied with him.

Chapter 23 of the Xunzi is titled "Human Nature Is Bad." Xunzi says people are born loving profit, feeling envy and wanting to please their eyes and ears. If they follow these, fighting and disorder follow. Goodness, he says, is the result of *conscious effort* (wei).

"Bad" here does not mean wicked from birth in every act. Many scholars translate the word e as "bad" or "crude." Xunzi means that raw desires, left unshaped, lead to conflict. His answer is teachers, ritual and law.

words.d: a Confucian thinker (c. 310–235 BCE) who argued human nature is bad; also his book
Xunzi's term (wei) for deliberate work that makes people good
a strong wish for something, such as food, gain or comfort

look.title: Nature and Effort
look.text: Human nature is bad; goodness is the result of conscious effort. People are born loving profit; if they follow this, strife arises and courtesy vanishes.
look.cite: Xunzi ch. 23, 'Human Nature Is Bad,' paraphrased; see Burton Watson, Hsün Tzu: Basic Writings (1963)
look.prompt: What does Xunzi think happens when people simply follow their desires? What does he offer instead?

check.q: What is the title of Xunzi chapter 23?
check.why: Chapter 23 of the Xunzi argues that human nature is bad.

check.q: According to Xunzi, where does goodness come from?
check.why: Xunzi says goodness is the product of deliberate effort (wei).

check.q: Which students does tradition link to Xunzi?
check.why: Tradition says the Legalists Han Feizi and Li Si studied with Xunzi.

lessons.title: Straightening Warped Wood
lessons.mainIdea: Xunzi compared people to warped wood and dull metal that become straight and sharp through steaming, pressing and grinding.
reading: Xunzi uses images from *craft*. A warped board must be steamed and clamped in a press frame before it is straight. Dull metal must be ground on a whetstone before it is sharp. In the same way, he says, people need teachers and ritual to become good.

His first chapter, "Encouraging Learning," opens with a famous line: learning must never stop. Blue dye comes from the indigo plant, yet it is bluer than the plant. Ice comes from water, yet it is colder. A student, shaped by learning, can surpass the teacher.

For Xunzi, *ritual* is the great human invention. The ancient sages, he says, saw that desires led to conflict and created rites to set limits and share goods fairly. Ritual does not destroy desire; it guides it.

words.d: skilled work with the hands, such as carpentry or metalwork
formal practices and rules of conduct; for Xunzi, a tool invented by sages to shape people

look.title: Two Gardeners
look.text: Gardener A: 'This seedling wants to grow tall. I water it and keep weeds away.' Gardener B: 'This vine would sprawl everywhere. I tie it to a trellis and prune it so it grows where it should.'
look.prompt: Which gardener sounds like Mencius and which like Xunzi? What does each image assume about human nature?

check.q: Which image does Xunzi use for shaping people?
check.why: Xunzi compares moral training to straightening warped wood in a press.

check.q: What does 'blue is bluer than indigo' mean in Xunzi?
choices: Learning can make a student surpass the teacher
check.why: In 'Encouraging Learning,' Xunzi uses it to show learning can take a student beyond the source.

check.q: For Xunzi, who created ritual?
check.why: Xunzi says the sages created rites to set limits on desire and prevent conflict.

lessons.title: One Tradition, Two Answers
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius and Xunzi both followed Confucius, and later readers mostly favored Mencius while still learning from Xunzi.
reading: Mencius and Xunzi agree on much. Both honor Confucius, value learning and ritual, and hope for humane rulers. Both think people can become sages. They *disagree* on where goodness starts: inside, as a sprout, or outside, through training.

Zhu Xi and the Song Neo-Confucians sided with Mencius. The Mencius became one of the Four Books, and Xunzi was left out. Some blamed Xunzi for his Legalist students. Yet Xunzi's views on ritual and learning shaped Confucian practice for centuries.

Modern readers revisit the debate. Some psychologists see sprouts of empathy in infants. Others stress how much children learn from their surroundings. Scholars caution against treating either ancient thinker as simply right; the *debate* itself is what the tradition keeps.

words.d: an exchange of reasons between people who disagree
later Confucian scholars, such as Zhu Xi, who renewed the tradition from the Song dynasty on
to hold different views

look.title: Two Confucians Compared
look.cite: Common scholarly estimates; see Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)

choices: Whether goodness starts inside or comes from training

check.q: Which thinker did Zhu Xi and the Neo-Confucians favor?
check.why: The Neo-Confucians sided with Mencius and made his book one of the Four Books.

check.q: How do scholars today tend to treat the debate?
choices: They study both sides rather than declare a winner
check.why: Scholars treat the debate as a living question and caution against declaring either side simply right.

choices: Nature tends to good like water flowing down
Human nature is bad; goodness comes from effort

Xunzi compares moral shaping to steaming and pressing warped wood.

review.why: In Mencius 6A, Mencius debates Gaozi's images of willow wood and whirling water.
